title: A practical way to think about trustworthy AI systems
summary: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organises AI risk work around governance, mapping, measurement and management. It provides a useful structure for thinking beyond model accuracy and considering how an AI system behaves in its real context.

title: Why model cards matter when AI systems reach real users
summary: Model cards document intended uses, limitations, training information and evaluation results. They help developers communicate what a model can and cannot safely support before it is integrated into a wider application.

title: Evaluation should be designed before an AI system is deployed
summary: Scikit-learn's evaluation guidance shows why the metric must match the task and the consequences of different errors. A single score rarely explains whether a system is reliable across classes, users and operating conditions.

title: Pipelines make machine-learning experiments easier to reproduce
summary: A pipeline keeps preprocessing and modelling steps together. This reduces leakage risk, makes cross-validation more reliable and creates a clearer path from experiment to a repeatable prediction service.

title: FastAPI connects AI experiments with usable applications
summary: FastAPI provides typed request validation, automatic API documentation and an efficient Python web layer. For AI applications, this can turn a notebook or model function into a service that other systems can test and use.

title: Experiment tracking keeps model decisions visible
summary: MLflow Tracking records parameters, code versions, metrics and output artefacts. That history makes it easier to compare experiments, explain why a model was selected and reproduce earlier results.

title: AI agents need boundaries as much as they need tools
summary: Agent guardrails can inspect inputs and outputs and stop a run when defined conditions are violated. This is important because tool access turns a language-model response into an action with real consequences.

title: Tool calling changes how an AI application should be evaluated
summary: Function calling lets a model request structured operations from application code. Reliable evaluation therefore has to examine tool choice, argument quality, execution errors and final-answer grounding rather than only the generated text.

title: The Model Context Protocol gives tools a common interface
summary: The Model Context Protocol defines a consistent way for AI applications to connect with tools and contextual data. A shared interface can reduce one-off integrations, but permissions and trust boundaries still require careful design.

title: Explainability is useful only when it answers the right clinical question
summary: SHAP estimates how features contribute to a model output. In healthcare work, those values can support investigation and communication, but they do not by themselves prove causality, clinical validity or safety.

title: Responsible healthcare AI begins with human oversight
summary: The World Health Organization's guidance places autonomy, safety, transparency, accountability, equity and sustainability at the centre of AI for health. These principles matter throughout design, evaluation and deployment.

title: Clinical prediction needs more than a good headline metric
summary: A classifier can rank cases correctly while still producing poorly calibrated probabilities. When predictions may inform clinical attention, probability calibration and threshold selection deserve separate evaluation.

title: RAG quality depends on retrieval before generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation places relevant external context in the model's prompt. If retrieval misses the right evidence, a fluent generator cannot reliably recover it, so retrieval and generation should be evaluated separately.

title: Document chunking is an engineering decision, not a fixed recipe
summary: Chunk size and document structure influence what a retrieval system can find and how much context a model receives. Layout, headings and semantic boundaries can be as important as a fixed token count.

title: Data versioning connects an ML result with its evidence
summary: DVC links data and pipeline stages with version-controlled metadata. This helps an ML team trace a result back to the dataset and processing steps that produced it without storing every large file directly in Git.

title: Transfer learning makes smaller vision datasets more practical
summary: Transfer learning starts from features learned on a larger dataset and adapts them to a new task. It can reduce training time and data requirements, although domain shift and class imbalance still need careful testing.

title: Image augmentation should reflect plausible variation
summary: Image augmentation introduces transformations during training to improve generalisation. The transformations should match realistic variation in the target setting rather than create images that could not occur in practice.

title: Computer-vision evaluation must look beyond overall accuracy
summary: Overall accuracy can hide poor performance on a smaller or more important class. Per-class precision, recall, confusion matrices and error review provide a more useful picture of vision-model behaviour.

title: Reproducible automation needs observable workflow runs
summary: Workflow history records when an automated process ran, which commit it used and where it failed. This turns a scheduled script into an observable process that can be checked and repaired.

title: Containers make an AI service easier to reproduce
summary: A container packages an application with its runtime dependencies. For AI services, this reduces environment differences between development, testing and deployment, although data and model artefacts still need explicit version control.

title: Semantic search depends on what an embedding preserves
summary: Sentence embeddings place text in a vector space where similarity can be measured. Their usefulness depends on the training objective, the target domain and whether the chosen similarity measure matches the retrieval task.
